Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does Prop. 5 solve?
In its current form, a state-level recall ballot asks two questions in sequence: first, whether to remove an elected official, and second, who should immediately replace them. Although removal requires a majority vote, replacement doesn’t; whoever gets the most votes takes office, even if it’s by a small plurality in a crowded field. That mismatch can mean that an officeholder ousted by majority vote can be replaced by someone with far less support, and it gives well-organized interest groups a powerful incentive to instigate a recall in order to install a preferred candidate who wouldn’t have majority support under normal conditions. Prop. 5 fixes that mismatch by removing the replacement question and filling a vacancy under existing succession law instead.

Why is this the best solution?
Prop. 5 is the best solution because it fixes the specific, politically exploitable flaw — the plurality replacement provision — while still maintaining the recall as a powerful tool of direct democracy. Under its provisions, if a governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor, already duly elected by a majority of Californians statewide, steps in. If a recall takes place in the first two years of the term and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election, voters would still get a special election for a permanent successor, with a runoff if needed to achieve a majority. If the recall takes place later in the term, the lieutenant governor would serve out the remainder of an ousted governor’s term, the same as if they were to leave office for some other reason. In the event of a recall of other state-level officers, those offices would be filled under existing vacancy replacement provisions.
Why would Californians want to remove someone from office but forfeit to the governor their current right to immediately choose a successor?
Two corrections worth making: In the event of a gubernatorial recall, it wouldn’t be the governor who gains power but the lieutenant governor, a separately elected constitutional officer who is, by virtue of California’s Constitution, explicitly and deliberately next in the line of succession. Intrinsic to any lieutenant governor’s campaign is the assertion that he or she is most qualified to step in if events so demand. Second, voters aren’t forfeiting a choice: If a governor is recalled early in their term, Californians would still elect a permanent successor by majority through a special election. This is a sensible change from the current format, where, in the event of a gubernatorial recall, a replacement candidate can become governor of the largest and most important state in the country with only a small plurality, in a special election decided by a reduced electorate in a low-information and highly politicized environment.
Explain how this empowers majority rule and why that matters.
As it currently stands, while recalling a state-level elected official requires majority support, replacing them doesn’t. Only a plurality is required, which could be as low as 20% in a crowded replacement field. Prop. 5 closes that gap. When a successor election is held, if no one wins a majority outright, it would go to a runoff. So, whoever ultimately holds the office would have secured the support of more than half the voters, not just the largest slice of a fractured field. This is the standard California already applies to nearly every other office and election scenario. A recall shouldn’t be the one process where a candidate can take power without the validation of majority voter support.

As it stands, a well-funded, motivated minority can force a recall and realistically expect its preferred candidate to win the replacement seat with a small plurality, sometimes far fewer votes than the officeholder who was removed. That’s a low bar for a high-value prize, and it’s why some recalls have been criticized as backdoor attempts to grab a seat that couldn’t be won in a regular election. Prop. 5 raises the bar and removes that incentive: Voters will still be able to remove a corrupt or malfeasant official, but it removes the strategic upside of gaming a plurality-only replacement. Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat. She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.” A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms. If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins. “I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said. California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election. This voter guide has everything you need to know The measure was placed on the November ballot by Democratic lawmakers in 2024 with the support of the secretary of state and good governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Voters. It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections. However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions. The ‘weak gazelle ’ Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman. In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 26 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes. Less than two weeks later, then-conservative commentator and now-San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014) told Orange County talk show hosts that gas tax opponents needed to use the “gazelle strategy,” to begin taking out lawmakers who’d approved the tax. Because he was elected by the slimmest margin of any senator, fewer than 2,500 votes. In the ensuing weeks, DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, led the effort to recall Newman, helping to collect more than 64,000 signatures — equivalent to 20% of voters in the last election — and centering its campaign on Newman’s “deciding vote” on the tax. Close to 60% of voters chose to recall Newman in June 2018, replacing him with Republican Ling Ling Chang. The recall ended the Democrats’ supermajority in the state Senate. Gov. Gray Davis speaks at an anti-recall labor union rally in San Jose on Oct. 5, 2003. Photo by David McNew, Getty Images In a recent interview with CalMatters, DeMaio stood by his “weak gazelle” strategy. “If voters want to stop something from happening and being repeated, then mid-term, sometimes the only thing they can do is to use a recall as a way of expressing their opposition,” he said. But Newman said that kind of “political gamesmanship” was not what former progressive governor Hiram Johnson intended when he proposed the law in 1911. In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.” Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill. “I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.” Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5. Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change. How would it work? If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election. If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election. If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change. “The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said. He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections. However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort. “It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.” A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.” Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions. In the ensuing weeks, DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, led the effort to recall Newman, helping to collect more than 64,000 signatures — equivalent to 20% of voters in the last election — and centering its campaign on Newman’s “deciding vote” on the tax. Close to 60% of voters chose to recall Newman in June 2018, replacing him with Republican Ling Ling Chang. The recall ended the Democrats’ supermajority in the state Senate. Gov. Gray Davis speaks at an anti-recall labor union rally in San Jose on Oct. 5, 2003. Photo by David McNew, Getty Images In a recent interview with CalMatters, DeMaio stood by his “weak gazelle” strategy. “If voters want to stop something from happening and being repeated, then mid-term, sometimes the only thing they can do is to use a recall as a way of expressing their opposition,” he said. But Newman said that kind of “political gamesmanship” was not what former progressive governor Hiram Johnson intended when he proposed the law in 1911. In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.” Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill. “I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.” Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5. Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change. How would it work? If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election. If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election. If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change. “The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said. He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections. However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort. “It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.” A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.” Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions. Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.

By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.

Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.

Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.

Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.

Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.

Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.

Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

But it is there. And the inability or unwillingness of lawmakers to put forth a simple, clean reform effort is reason enough for voters to reject this measure.
California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does Prop. 5 solve?
In its current form, a state-level recall ballot asks two questions in sequence: first, whether to remove an elected official, and second, who should immediately replace them. Although removal requires a majority vote, replacement doesn’t; whoever gets the most votes takes office, even if it’s by a small plurality in a crowded field. That mismatch can mean that an officeholder ousted by majority vote can be replaced by someone with far less support, and it gives well-organized interest groups a powerful incentive to instigate a recall in order to install a preferred candidate who wouldn’t have majority support under normal conditions. Prop. 5 fixes that mismatch by removing the replacement question and filling a vacancy under existing succession law instead.

Why is this the best solution?
Prop. 5 is the best solution because it fixes the specific, politically exploitable flaw — the plurality replacement provision — while still maintaining the recall as a powerful tool of direct democracy. Under its provisions, if a governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor, already duly elected by a majority of Californians statewide, steps in. If a recall takes place in the first two years of the term and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election, voters would still get a special election for a permanent successor, with a runoff if needed to achieve a majority. If the recall takes place later in the term, the lieutenant governor would serve out the remainder of an ousted governor’s term, the same as if they were to leave office for some other reason. In the event of a recall of other state-level officers, those offices would be filled under existing vacancy replacement provisions.
Why would Californians want to remove someone from office but forfeit to the governor their current right to immediately choose a successor?
Two corrections worth making: In the event of a gubernatorial recall, it wouldn’t be the governor who gains power but the lieutenant governor, a separately elected constitutional officer who is, by virtue of California’s Constitution, explicitly and deliberately next in the line of succession. Intrinsic to any lieutenant governor’s campaign is the assertion that he or she is most qualified to step in if events so demand. Second, voters aren’t forfeiting a choice: If a governor is recalled early in their term, Californians would still elect a permanent successor by majority through a special election. This is a sensible change from the current format, where, in the event of a gubernatorial recall, a replacement candidate can become governor of the largest and most important state in the country with only a small plurality, in a special election decided by a reduced electorate in a low-information and highly politicized environment.
Explain how this empowers majority rule and why that matters.
As it currently stands, while recalling a state-level elected official requires majority support, replacing them doesn’t. Only a plurality is required, which could be as low as 20% in a crowded replacement field. Prop. 5 closes that gap. When a successor election is held, if no one wins a majority outright, it would go to a runoff. So, whoever ultimately holds the office would have secured the support of more than half the voters, not just the largest slice of a fractured field. This is the standard California already applies to nearly every other office and election scenario. A recall shouldn’t be the one process where a candidate can take power without the validation of majority voter support.
How does this measure stop political groups from abusing the recall process?
It removes the existing incentive for political gamesmanship at the expense of electoral integrity. As it stands, a well-funded, motivated minority can force a recall and realistically expect its preferred candidate to win the replacement seat with a small plurality, sometimes far fewer votes than the officeholder who was removed. That’s a low bar for a high-value prize, and it’s why some recalls have been criticized as backdoor attempts to grab a seat that couldn’t be won in a regular election. Prop. 5 raises the bar and removes that incentive: Voters will still be able to remove a corrupt or malfeasant official, but it removes the strategic upside of gaming a plurality-only replacement. Instead, a replacement would be made in the normal order, and in the next election, the winner would ultimately secure a majority, with a runoff if needed.
How would this save taxpayers money?

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does Prop. 5 solve?
In its current form, a state-level recall ballot asks two questions in sequence: first, whether to remove an elected official, and second, who should immediately replace them. Although removal requires a majority vote, replacement doesn’t; whoever gets the most votes takes office, even if it’s by a small plurality in a crowded field. That mismatch can mean that an officeholder ousted by majority vote can be replaced by someone with far less support, and it gives well-organized interest groups a powerful incentive to instigate a recall in order to install a preferred candidate who wouldn’t have majority support under normal conditions. Prop. 5 fixes that mismatch by removing the replacement question and filling a vacancy under existing succession law instead.

We asked the No on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
Why is this the best solution?
Prop. 5 is the best solution because it fixes the specific, politically exploitable flaw — the plurality replacement provision — while still maintaining the recall as a powerful tool of direct democracy. Under its provisions, if a governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor, already duly elected by a majority of Californians statewide, steps in. If a recall takes place in the first two years of the term and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election, voters would still get a special election for a permanent successor, with a runoff if needed to achieve a majority. If the recall takes place later in the term, the lieutenant governor would serve out the remainder of an ousted governor’s term, the same as if they were to leave office for some other reason. In the event of a recall of other state-level officers, those offices would be filled under existing vacancy replacement provisions.
Why would Californians want to remove someone from office but forfeit to the governor their current right to immediately choose a successor?
Two corrections worth making: In the event of a gubernatorial recall, it wouldn’t be the governor who gains power but the lieutenant governor, a separately elected constitutional officer who is, by virtue of California’s Constitution, explicitly and deliberately next in the line of succession. Intrinsic to any lieutenant governor’s campaign is the assertion that he or she is most qualified to step in if events so demand. Second, voters aren’t forfeiting a choice: If a governor is recalled early in their term, Californians would still elect a permanent successor by majority through a special election. This is a sensible change from the current format, where, in the event of a gubernatorial recall, a replacement candidate can become governor of the largest and most important state in the country with only a small plurality, in a special election decided by a reduced electorate in a low-information and highly politicized environment.
Explain how this empowers majority rule and why that matters.
As it currently stands, while recalling a state-level elected official requires majority support, replacing them doesn’t. Only a plurality is required, which could be as low as 20% in a crowded replacement field. Prop. 5 closes that gap. When a successor election is held, if no one wins a majority outright, it would go to a runoff. So, whoever ultimately holds the office would have secured the support of more than half the voters, not just the largest slice of a fractured field. This is the standard California already applies to nearly every other office and election scenario. A recall shouldn’t be the one process where a candidate can take power without the validation of majority voter support.
How does this measure stop political groups from abusing the recall process?
It removes the existing incentive for political gamesmanship at the expense of electoral integrity. As it stands, a well-funded, motivated minority can force a recall and realistically expect its preferred candidate to win the replacement seat with a small plurality, sometimes far fewer votes than the officeholder who was removed. That’s a low bar for a high-value prize, and it’s why some recalls have been criticized as backdoor attempts to grab a seat that couldn’t be won in a regular election. Prop. 5 raises the bar and removes that incentive: Voters will still be able to remove a corrupt or malfeasant official, but it removes the strategic upside of gaming a plurality-only replacement. Instead, a replacement would be made in the normal order, and in the next election, the winner would ultimately secure a majority, with a runoff if needed.
How would this save taxpayers money?
First and foremost, by changing the incentive structure by eliminating the second question, Prop. 5 would save taxpayers money by reducing the likelihood of hyperpartisan recalls like the one which targeted Gov. Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat. She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.” A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms. If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins. “I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said. California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election. It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections. However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions. The ‘weak gazelle ’ Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman. In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 26 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes. Less than two weeks later, then-conservative commentator and now-San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014) told Orange County talk show hosts that gas tax opponents needed to use the “gazelle strategy,” to begin taking out lawmakers who’d approved the tax. In the ensuing weeks, DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, led the effort to recall Newman, helping to collect more than 64,000 signatures — equivalent to 20% of voters in the last election — and centering its campaign on Newman’s “deciding vote” on the tax. But Newman said that kind of “political gamesmanship” was not what former progressive governor Hiram Johnson intended when he proposed the law in 1911. In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.” Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill. “I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.” Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5. Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change. How would it work? If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election. If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election. If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change. “The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said. He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections. However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort. “It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.” A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.” Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions. Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.

By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.

Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.

Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.

Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does Prop. 5 solve?
In its current form, a state-level recall ballot asks two questions in sequence: first, whether to remove an elected official, and second, who should immediately replace them. Although removal requires a majority vote, replacement doesn’t; whoever gets the most votes takes office, even if it’s by a small plurality in a crowded field. That mismatch can mean that an officeholder ousted by majority vote can be replaced by someone with far less support, and it gives well-organized interest groups a powerful incentive to instigate a recall in order to install a preferred candidate who wouldn’t have majority support under normal conditions. Prop. 5 fixes that mismatch by removing the replacement question and filling a vacancy under existing succession law instead.
Related Articles
We asked the No on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
Why is this the best solution?
Prop. 5 is the best solution because it fixes the specific, politically exploitable flaw — the plurality replacement provision — while still maintaining the recall as a powerful tool of direct democracy. Under its provisions, if a governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor, already duly elected by a majority of Californians statewide, steps in. If a recall takes place in the first two years of the term and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election, voters would still get a special election for a permanent successor, with a runoff if needed to achieve a majority. If the recall takes place later in the term, the lieutenant governor would serve out the remainder of an ousted governor’s term, the same as if they were to leave office for some other reason. In the event of a recall of other state-level officers, those offices would be filled under existing vacancy replacement provisions.
Why would Californians want to remove someone from office but forfeit to the governor their current right to immediately choose a successor?
Two corrections worth making: In the event of a gubernatorial recall, it wouldn’t be the governor who gains power but the lieutenant governor, a separately elected constitutional officer who is, by virtue of California’s Constitution, explicitly and deliberately next in the line of succession. Intrinsic to any lieutenant governor’s campaign is the assertion that he or she is most qualified to step in if events so demand. Second, voters aren’t forfeiting a choice: If a governor is recalled early in their term, Californians would still elect a permanent successor by majority through a special election. This is a sensible change from the current format, where, in the event of a gubernatorial recall, a replacement candidate can become governor of the largest and most important state in the country with only a small plurality, in a special election decided by a reduced electorate in a low-information and highly politicized environment.
Explain how this empowers majority rule and why that matters.
As it currently stands, while recalling a state-level elected official requires majority support, replacing them doesn’t. Only a plurality is required, which could be as low as 20% in a crowded replacement field. Prop. 5 closes that gap. When a successor election is held, if no one wins a majority outright, it would go to a runoff. So, whoever ultimately holds the office would have secured the support of more than half the voters, not just the largest slice of a fractured field. This is the standard California already applies to nearly every other office and election scenario. A recall shouldn’t be the one process where a candidate can take power without the validation of majority voter support.
How does this measure stop political groups from abusing the recall process?
It removes the existing incentive for political gamesmanship at the expense of electoral integrity. As it stands, a well-funded, motivated minority can force a recall and realistically expect its preferred candidate to win the replacement seat with a small plurality, sometimes far fewer votes than the officeholder who was removed. That’s a low bar for a high-value prize, and it’s why some recalls have been criticized as backdoor attempts to grab a seat that couldn’t be won in a regular election. Prop. 5 raises the bar and removes that incentive: Voters will still be able to remove a corrupt or malfeasant official, but it removes the strategic upside of gaming a plurality-only replacement. Instead, a replacement would be made in the normal order, and in the next election, the winner would ultimately secure a majority, with a runoff if needed.
How would this save taxpayers money?

PROPOSITION 5
This amendment proposed by Senate Constitutional
Amendment 1 of the 2023–2024 Regular Session
(Resolution Chapter 204, Statutes of 2024) expressly
amends the California Constitution by amending
sections thereof; therefore, existing provisions
proposed to be deleted are printed in strikeout type
and new provisions proposed to be added are printed in
italic type to indicate that they are new.
PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO
ARTICLES II AND V
First—That Section 15 of Article II thereof is amended
to read:
SEC. 15. (a) An election to determine whether to
recall an officer and, if appropriate, to elect a successor
shall be called by the Governor and held not less than
60 days nor more than 80 days from the date of
certification of sufficient signatures.
(b) A recall election may be conducted within 180 days
from the date of certification of sufficient signatures in
order that the election may be consolidated with the
next regularly scheduled election occurring wholly or
partially within the same jurisdiction in which the recall
election is held, if the number of voters eligible to vote
at that next regularly scheduled election equal at least
50 percent of all the voters eligible to vote at the recall
election.
(c) If the majority vote on the question is to recall, the
officer is removed and, if there is a candidate, the
candidate who receives a plurality is the successor. The
officer may not be a candidate, nor shall there be any
candidacy for an office filled pursuant to subdivision (d)
of Section 16 of Article VI. and the office shall be
vacant. The vacancy shall be filled in accordance with
this Constitution and statute, provided that the officer
who was the subject of the recall election shall not be
appointed to fill the vacancy in that office.
118 | Text of Proposed Laws
Second—That Section 17 of Article II thereof is
amended to read:
SEC. 17. If recall of the Governor or Secretary of
State is initiated, the recall duties of that office shall be
performed by the Lieutenant Governor Secretary of
State or Controller, respectively. If recalls of the
Governor and Secretary of State are initiated at the
same time, the recall duties of both offices shall be
performed by the Controller.
Third—That Section 10 of Article V thereof is amended
to read:
SEC. 10. (a) The Lieutenant Governor shall become
Governor when a vacancy occurs in the office of
Governor.
(b) Notwithstanding subdivision (c) of Section 15 of
Article II, if the Governor is removed from office by
recall, the Lieutenant Governor shall become Governor
for the remainder of the unexpired term. If the Governor
is removed from office by recall before the close of the
nomination period for the next statewide election during
the first two years of the Governor’s term, a special
election shall be called to replace the Governor and
shall be consolidated with the statewide primary
election and, if necessary, the subsequent statewide
general election. If a candidate receives a majority of
the votes in the special election that is consolidated
with the statewide primary election, that candidate
shall become Governor for the remainder of the
unexpired term. If no candidate receives a majority of
the votes, the top two vote-getters shall compete in a
special election consolidated with the subsequent
statewide general election, and the winner of that
election shall become Governor for the remainder of the
unexpired term.
(c) The Lieutenant Governor shall act as Governor
during the impeachment, absence from the State, or
other temporary disability of the Governor or of a
Governor-elect who fails to take office.
(d) The Legislature shall provide an order of
precedence after the Lieutenant Governor for
succession to the office of Governor and for the
temporary exercise of the Governor’s functions.
(e) The Supreme Court has exclusive jurisdiction to
determine all questions arising under this section.
(f) Standing to raise questions of vacancy or temporary
disability is vested exclusively in a body provided by
statute.
PROPOSITION 37
This initiative measure is submitted to the people in
accordance with the provisions of Section 8 of Article II
of the California Constitution.
This initiative measure adds sections to the Health and
Safety Code; therefore, new provisions proposed to be
added are printed in italic type to indicate that they are
new.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
What problem would Prop. 5 create?
A disincentive for the people to self-govern, leading to more distrust of government and restlessness of the “masses.” After a time of withdrawal and lack of participation, the people will feel and react to their oppression in a negative way. Oppressed people eventually revolt, and it’s never pretty.

We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
Currently, the recall process allows a candidate to win office without a majority. Why is that a system not worth reforming?
Under the current system, the democratic process of self-governance is served, and infinite amounts of taxpayer funds are saved by the current one-step process.
Prop. 5 “reforms” the current process by taking power from the people, and — worse — punishing the people for having the audacity to self-govern.
In the case of a recall, the term of office is limited to the remainder of the term of the recalled individual, and awarding the win to the person receiving a plurality in a crowded field is much more protective of the “democratic process” than adopting the changes proposed by Prop. 5, where the Sacramento insiders are the winners, hundreds of millions of dollars are wasted, and democracy dies.
If this measure isn’t a solution for fixing the recall process, do you have an alternate proposal?
This question pre-supposes the recall process needs fixing. The current process, wherein a recall decision and a filling of the recalled position in the case of recall success on the same ballot is efficient, fiscally responsible and respectful to the public.
The suggestion that the cost of having part two of the recall ballot is negligible, let alone millions of dollars, is patently absurd. Also absurd is the Prop. 5 proposal to eventually fill the recalled position with another, delayed election. The cost of a second election, which is likely to lead to a runoff costing more millions, is unarguable. That’s the very definition of absurd.
To quote Sen. Jones, “Our recall process is only ‘broke’ for those who find themselves on the business end of it, like Proposition 5’s author did when he (voted to raise) taxes after breaking campaign promises.”
What’s the biggest misconception about Prop. 5?
That there’s something wrong with the current system, and that CA legislators have any respect for a government of, by and for the people. CA is no longer a republic, but a socialist oligarchy. The power of the people to govern themselves has been so diminished already as to be virtually eliminated, and Prop. 5 is another step to seal the deal for complete power of the elite.
What did we miss? What didn’t we ask that our readers should know?
The element of Prop. 5 dealing with gubernatorial succession is also faulty. Yes, the people ostensibly elected a lieutenant governor, to serve as governor in the event of incapacity or death of the elected governor, not in the event of the governor’s disgrace — by which the lieutenant governor is surely tainted.
If the lieutenant governor wishes to succeed the governor in the event of a recall, that person may appear on the second portion of the ballot.
Chances are virtually 100% that if the people have grown disenchanted with the governor’s performance, they will be equally unwilling to be represented in that office by the second in command — almost certainly complicit in every act of disappointment and betrayal by the governor.

## LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST
The California Constitution provides that voters may recall a state officer by majority vote and, in the same election, elect a successor with a plurality of the vote.
The Constitution prohibits an officer who is the subject of a recall election from being a candidate for successor.
The Constitution also prohibits a successor candidacy for the office of judge of the Supreme Court or a court of appeal.
...
This measure would provide, in the event an officer is removed in a recall election, for the office to remain vacant until a successor candidate to hold the unexpired term of the office receives a majority of votes at a special election, or for the office to remain vacant for the remainder of the term if there is insufficient time to hold a special election, as specified.* the nomination period for the subsequent term of that office has closed.* The measure would allow an officer who was the subject of the recall election to be a candidate in the special election.
The measure would require the Legislature to enact laws providing for the election of a successor.

PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO

First—That Section 15 of Article II thereof is amended
to read:
SEC. 15. (a) An election to determine whether to
recall an officer and, if appropriate, to elect a successor
shall be called by the Governor and held not less than
60 days nor more than 80 days from the date of

(b) A recall election may be conducted within 180 days

order that the election may be consolidated with the
next regularly scheduled election occurring wholly or
partially within the same jurisdiction in which the recall
election is held, if the number of voters eligible to vote
at that next regularly scheduled election equal at least
50 percent of all the voters eligible to vote at the recall
election.
(c) If the majority vote on the question is to recall, the
officer is removed and, if there is a candidate, the
candidate who receives a plurality is the successor. The
officer may not be a candidate, nor shall there be any
candidacy for an office filled pursuant to subdivision (d)
of Section 16 of Article VI. and the office shall be
vacant. The vacancy shall be filled in accordance with
this Constitution and statute, provided that the officer
who was the subject of the recall election shall not be
appointed to fill the vacancy in that office.

disability is vested exclusively in a body provided by

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
What problem would Prop. 5 create?
A disincentive for the people to self-govern, leading to more distrust of government and restlessness of the “masses.” After a time of withdrawal and lack of participation, the people will feel and react to their oppression in a negative way. Oppressed people eventually revolt, and it’s never pretty.
